entities.summary:
Pedro Ferris (1416–1478) was a Spanish Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal who played a crucial role in the Catholic Church's response to the Ottoman Empire's expansion into Eastern Europe. During his tenure as Cardinal, he was instrumental in convening several high-profile synods aimed at strengthening the Church's stance against the Ottoman threat. His efforts contributed to the creation of the Confraternity of Christendom, a powerful alliance between European Christian states that would shape the course of European politics for centuries to come.

Ferris's influence extended beyond his ecclesiastical duties, as he was also a patron of the arts and education. He supported several prominent artists and scholars, including the renowned humanist scholar, Juan de Torquemada. This patronage helped foster a cultural renaissance in Spain, which would have far-reaching consequences for European culture and society.

Despite his significant contributions to the Catholic Church, Ferris's legacy is also marked by controversy. His involvement in the Inquisition, a tribunal established to root out heresy and dissent within the Church, has been widely criticized as a tool of oppression and intolerance. Nevertheless, Ferris's efforts to reform the Inquisition and promote greater tolerance within the Church remain an important chapter in his story.

In the end, Ferris's life was cut short by the Black Death, which swept through Europe in 1478, claiming millions of lives and leaving a lasting impact on European society. His death marked the beginning of a new era for the Catholic Church, one that would be shaped by the challenges posed by the plague and the growing tensions between Christianity and Islam.
